questions.topic: A qualified transcription in a reconstructed scene
questions.learningObjective: Recognise how a qualified transcription marks a reconstructed scene
questions.stem: In the logbook, Marta reconstructs a conversation between two beekeepers, marking the words she cannot vouch for with brackets.

options.text: Bracketing marks the reconstructed words, so the report admits its inferences without losing the source.
Brackets are a printing convention borrowed from older books, and the log should use quotation marks instead.
options.misconception: treats the marker as a borrowed printing habit

options.text: Brackets show that the whole scene is doubtful, so nothing in it should be taken as evidence of anything.
options.misconception: reads one marked detail as discrediting the whole scene

options.text: Brackets are unnecessary because a beekeeper's logbook is already known to contain a good deal of guesswork.
options.misconception: assumes the reader already discounts everything in a logbook

questions.explanation: The bracket marks exactly which words are inferred, so recorded and supplied material stay distinguishable. B misreads the mark as a habit, C makes it discredit everything, and D removes the need to mark at all.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The licence an interview provides
questions.learningObjective: Determine what licence an interview provides
questions.stem: The logbook notes that a newspaper interview was conducted on condition the reporter could quote only two of the answers.

answer.exemplar: An interview licence sets the boundary of what may be published, not a measure of what is true. A condition that limits quotation limits the use of the answers, and the writer has to honour it even where a fuller version would serve the argument better. Quoting beyond the licence is a breach of the arrangement regardless of how accurate the material is or how good the resulting passage sounds.

questions.explanation: The licence limits use, not accuracy, so material outside it cannot appear in the piece however true it is. Treating the arrangement as merely a matter of taste would be a breach of the terms it was granted under.
questions.hint: Distinguish what is true from what is permitted.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a profile has still left unexamined
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a profile has still left unexamined
questions.stem: A profile in the logbook describes a comb maker's working method, her hours, her business, and her opinion of the season.

answer.exemplar: A profile can describe a person's working life in full detail and still leave the questions that matter most untouched, because the form is organised around what a reporter can observe and elicit. Hours, method and opinion are all available; the reasons behind a decision, or the pressures the subject will not name, are not. Naming what the piece leaves out is part of describing it honestly rather than a complaint about its length.

questions.explanation: Detail and depth are different axes: a profile can be rich in observation and still silent on the subject's reasons and pressures. Its limits follow from what the form can reach, not from carelessness.
questions.hint: Ask what the form cannot reach.

options.misconception: defers judgement to the maker's own printed disclaimers

options.text: The review is sound, because a review of one product is not a review of a whole category of tools.
options.misconception: narrows the duty by treating the review as a single-item report

options.text: The review commits to a judgement about suitability, so silence on a known limitation leaves it incomplete.

questions.explanation: A verdict about suitability implies a verdict about what the tool cannot do, and the review leaves that half unsaid. A, B and C each shrink the review's duty to fit what it has written.

questions.topic: Two criteria and their weighting
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two criteria against their stated weighting
questions.stem: A tool review in the logbook says the hive tool is light but slow to work, and gives no sense of which matters more for the writer.

answer.exemplar: Two criteria only decide a verdict when their relative weight is settled. Lightness and speed pull in opposite directions here, so the review's silence on which one matters for a small apiary leaves the verdict unsupported. A usable judgement either states the weighting, or shows the outcome is the same under any plausible weighting, and until one of those is done the reader has no way to act on what is written.

questions.explanation: Without a weighting, the two criteria point opposite ways and the verdict is unsupported unless it holds either way. Stating the weighting, or showing the result is weight-independent, is what settles it.
questions.hint: Say which criterion carries the verdict.

questions.topic: Consent steps in an interview-based article
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the consent steps an interview-based article needs
questions.stem: A logbook draft publishes an interview in which a speaker is named, without recording that any consent was sought.

answer.exemplar: Consent is a sequence of steps, not a single yes: the speaker must be asked, must understand what the piece is for, and must agree to the terms that follow, and the writer has to show that each step happened. questions.explanation: Each consent step answers a different question, and the article records none of them, so its claim to be working with an agreeing speaker rests on nothing. Recording the sequence is what makes the consent visible.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a profile has still left unexamined
questions.stem: One profile in the logbook quotes the maker at length on her comb designs and says nothing about why she stopped selling them.

answer.exemplar: A profile works under a constraint of representativeness: it must present the subject as someone might recognise, which means naming the pressures and choices that shaped them, not only the work they are known for. questions.stem: A logbook reconstruction of a growers' meeting gives both speakers' words but brackets the sentences where a position was left unsaid.

answer.exemplar: A qualified transcription reports what was said and marks the parts where the source does not settle what happened, so a reader can see where the record stops and inference begins. questions.explanation: Marking the uncertain passages keeps the reconstruction from presenting inference as testimony. It shows the reader where the record ends, which is exactly what a qualified transcription promises.

questions.stem: A review in the logbook states that a book is the best available introduction to the subject and gives three paragraphs of evidence.

options.text: The constraint rules out one source of material, so the writer must build the portrait from the business itself.

questions.explanation: A ban on quotation removes the subject's own voice and obliges the writer to work from observable material. Paraphrase, a substitute statement and familiar format are all ways of keeping what the brief removed.
questions.hint: Ask what the brief removes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a profile has still left unexamined
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a profile has still left unexamined

stimulus.body: The profile is 1,900 words and mentions the extractor, the trailer, the queens and the prices. It does not mention that the yard was shut for two winters and that the reason was never given to me. My editor asks whether the profile is honest about that, and I do not have an answer.

questions.stem: What does this note identify about the profile?

options.text: The profile leaves the two shut winters unexamined, so it presents a working life without the gap in it.
The note identifies a problem of length, since a profile of 1,900 words cannot be fair to a complex subject.
options.misconception: redirects the fault from silence to length

options.text: The note identifies a problem of sources, since the profile never says who supplied the prices.
options.misconception: faults unattributed detail rather than the missing history

options.text: The note identifies a problem of tone, since the profile reads as an advertisement for the business.
options.misconception: faults the tone instead of the omission

questions.explanation: Two shut winters and an unexplained absence are part of the working life the profile presents, and it does not show them. Length, sourcing and tone are complaints the note does not make.
questions.hint: Ask what the profile presents as a working life.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a review commits itself to
questions.learningObjective: State what a review commits itself to
questions.stem: Another review in the logbook calls a book the best available introduction to the subject, and admits it assumes the reader already knows one term.

answer.exemplar: A review commits itself to a comparative judgement and to the reader it addresses, and this one claims the highest place among introductions while quietly narrowing who can use the book. Those two commitments pull against each other, because an introduction that needs a term explained is not yet available to the reader who has most need of it. The review could keep both claims only by saying that the term is explained elsewhere in the book, and it does not.

questions.explanation: Calling a book the best introduction and making it unusable for a beginner are hard to hold together, so the review owes an explanation of the term. Silence lets the reader assume compatibility that may not exist.
questions.hint: Ask who the book is actually for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two criteria and their weighting
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two criteria against their stated weighting
questions.stem: One review in the logbook weighs a bee suit on warmth and on price, and its verdict would be the same whichever way they were weighted.

options.text: The weighting does not matter here, since a verdict that survives any weighting needs no argument about criteria at all.
options.misconception: treats weighting as irrelevant whenever a verdict seems stable

options.text: The weighting does not matter here, because the two criteria point the same way for this suit.
The weighting matters more than usual, since the two criteria pull against each other and one must dominate.
options.misconception: assumes criteria must conflict

options.text: The weighting matters more than usual, because a reader who disagrees with the weight should reach a different verdict.
options.misconception: assumes a sensitive verdict is a defective one

questions.explanation: When both criteria favour the same verdict, the weighting cannot change the outcome, so the review may leave it unstated. A and C generalise from a special case, and D treats a stable verdict as a flaw.
questions.hint: Ask whether the criteria point the same way.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A qualified transcription in a reconstructed scene
questions.learningObjective: Recognise how a qualified transcription marks a reconstructed scene
questions.stem: A further page in the logbook reconstructs a conversation and marks the doubtful lines, but leaves out the silence that followed the question.

answer.exemplar: Qualifying the words a record supports is only half of the honesty a reconstruction owes, because the unmarked parts of a scene still assert something. A silence after a question carries weight in any exchange, and leaving it out while marking the words constructs a scene that is more certain than the evidence allows. The bracket tells a reader where the record is thin; the omitted silence is a thinner place the reader cannot see.

questions.explanation: Marking the doubtful words helps, but the omitted silence still asserts a scene the record does not support. A qualified reconstruction has to show where the record is thin, not only in words.
questions.hint: Ask what the unmarked parts still assert.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The licence an interview provides
questions.learningObjective: Determine what licence an interview provides
questions.stem: Another note in the logbook records that an interview was granted on condition that the subject's name not appear, and the article describes the subject's house instead.

options.text: The article is sound, because the condition named names and the piece contains no name.
options.misconception: reads compliance with the letter as compliance with the condition

options.text: The article is sound, because describing a house is a standard opening and no rule was given against it.
options.misconception: treats a standard opening as beyond the terms of the agreement

options.text: The description identifies the subject as surely as a name would, so the condition is broken by the writing.
The article is sound, because a reader who recognises the house already had the name in memory.
options.misconception: blames the reader's memory for the identification

questions.explanation: A condition against identification is broken by an identifying description whatever wording is used. Letter of the rule, standard openings and the reader's own memory do not restore what the description took away.
questions.hint: Ask what the description identifies.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Consent steps in an interview-based article
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the consent steps an interview-based article needs

stimulus.body: Consent note: asked, purpose explained, name declined, photographs refused. Quote agreed for the piece, subject asked to see the paragraph before publication. I have the note in the back of this book, dated 3 March, and I have not yet sent her the paragraph.

questions.stem: What is outstanding on this page?

options.text: Nothing at all, since every consent step was recorded on the date it was made.
options.misconception: treats a record of steps as the completion of them

options.text: The subject's agreement to be quoted, since the note mentions quoting without recording a decision on it.
options.misconception: reads a stated agreement as an absent one

options.text: The legal form, since a consent note in a personal book has no standing without a witness's signature.
options.misconception: raises a formality the note never promised to satisfy

options.text: The agreed final step, since the subject asked to see the paragraph and that has not yet happened.

questions.explanation: The note records the steps agreed and one still to be performed, which is the paragraph the subject asked to see. Completion, a missing agreement and legal formality are all things this page does not raise.
questions.hint: Ask which agreed step has not happened.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The constraint a profile works under
questions.learningObjective: Apply the constraint a profile works under
questions.stem: One profile in the logbook is commissioned on the condition that it describe a beekeeper's technique rather than her business.

answer.exemplar: A profile written under this constraint has to find the person in the work, which is harder than it sounds and gives the writer a problem of evidence: technique can be described from observation, but the person inside it has to be inferred from what she does and how she explains it. A piece that reports the technique accurately and says nothing about the person will have met the brief and will also have failed at it, because the brief asked for a portrait and not a manual.

questions.explanation: The brief names the field and the subject at once, so technique must be the route to the person, not a substitute for one. Meeting the brief only in its first half leaves the profile without its subject.
questions.hint: Ask how the brief is about a person.
